How to Become a Frontend Developer: A Practical Roadmap (From My Own Journey)

A practical roadmap to become a frontend developer: what to learn, in what order, how to build a portfolio and land your first job — based on my own path.

NM Nipun Mitra ·26 October 2026 ·2 min read

If you’re wondering how to become a frontend developer, here’s the honest answer: you don’t need to be a genius, and you don’t need to learn everything. You need the fundamentals, a lot of practice, and real projects you can show.

My own path: I studied a Diploma in Computer Technology at Magura Polytechnic Institute, took courses in frontend development and later PHP and Laravel, and got my first job as a frontend developer at Mamurjor IT, where I built more than twenty client websites. Today I work at CodeWare Ltd building Next.js applications, while finishing my B.Sc. in CSE. This is the roadmap I’d follow if I were starting again.

Step 1: HTML and CSS — properly

Learn semantic HTML (headings, lists, forms, buttons, landmarks) and modern CSS: the box model, Flexbox, Grid and responsive design with media queries. Rebuild real websites you like, section by section. This is the foundation everything else stands on.

Step 2: JavaScript fundamentals

Variables, functions, arrays and objects, the DOM, events, fetch and promises, async/await. Build small interactive things: a to-do list, a weather app using an API, a quiz, a filterable product list.

Step 3: Developer tools

  • Git and GitHub — commit every day; your GitHub becomes part of your portfolio.
  • VS Code and the browser DevTools.
  • The terminal and npm basics.
  • Figma — enough to read designs and inspect spacing and colours.

Step 4: A framework — React, then Next.js

Once JavaScript feels comfortable, learn React: components, props, state, effects and forms. Then Next.js for routing, server rendering and building real, SEO-friendly sites. Add TypeScript as soon as you can — it’s expected in most professional teams.

Step 5: Styling at speed

Learn Tailwind CSS and at least one component library. Bootstrap is still common in many companies too. The goal is to turn a design into a pixel-perfect, responsive page quickly.

Step 6: Build a portfolio that gets interviews

  • 3–5 solid projects beat 20 tutorial clones.
  • Make at least one project that uses a real API, forms and authentication.
  • Deploy everything with a live link.
  • Write a short case study: the problem, your approach, what you learned.
  • Keep your own portfolio site fast, responsive and accessible — it’s your first impression.

Step 7: Land your first job

Apply widely, including smaller agencies and IT companies — they often give juniors the most varied experience. Practise explaining your projects, be honest about what you don’t know yet, and show that you learn quickly. Freelance projects for local businesses are also great real-world experience.

Keep growing

After your first job, go deeper: performance, accessibility, testing, state management, APIs and a backend framework like Laravel or Node.js. Many frontend developers grow into full-stack or web app development roles this way.

Questions about getting started? Feel free to reach out — I remember how confusing the beginning can be.

Frequently asked questions

How long does it take to become a frontend developer?

With consistent daily practice, many people become job-ready for a junior role in roughly one year. The key is building real projects, not just watching tutorials.

Do I need a computer science degree to become a frontend developer?

No. A degree helps, but many developers start with a diploma, courses or self-study. Employers mostly look at what you can build — a strong portfolio and real projects matter most.

Should I learn React or plain JavaScript first?

Learn plain JavaScript first. Understanding the DOM, events, arrays, objects and async code makes React much easier and helps you debug problems later.
